shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ at market exchange rates (NGDPDPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Sixteen times. {p} In 1990, the average Japanese person produced sixteen times as much as the average Pole, in plain dollars: about twenty-six thousand four hundred dollars a year, against one thousand six hundred. {pp} This year, in the IMF's numbers: about thirty-five thousand four hundred in Japan, thirty-one thousand two hundred in Poland. Japan is about fourteen percent ahead. {p} And by 2031, in the IMF's forecast, the gap is two hundred and fifty-six dollars.

This year, on income adjusted for prices, the IMF's numbers put Poland ahead of Japan. That was one of the biggest stories on this channel. But adjusted for prices isn't the money people see on a payslip converted into dollars. {p} So here's the plain money: market exchange rates, no adjustment. {pp} <soft>And the surprising part of this chart isn't Poland. It's Japan. In plain dollars, the average Japanese person produces less this year than in 1995.</soft>
Quick one before the chart: this channel is a series about who's passing whom. Subscribe so you don't miss the next one. {p} Now, the long view.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · Poland's GDP per capita in current US$, as % of Japan's; 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Here's Poland as a share of Japan, in plain dollars. {p} 1990: six percent. In 1990, the average Japanese person produced more than the average American. Poland was coming out of communism. {p} By 2004, when Poland joined the European Union, it was at seventeen percent. 2012: twenty-six. {pp} Then the line turns almost straight up. Fifty-three percent in 2022. Seventy-four in 2024. Eighty-eight this year. That's thirty-five points in four years. Poland didn't suddenly get that much faster. Something happened to Japan.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ at market exchange rates (NGDPDPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Here's Japan alone, in plain dollars per person. {p} 1995: about forty-five thousand. Then thirty years of going sideways. The peak came in 2012, at almost fifty thousand. {pp} And then, from 2012 to 2024, it fell by almost a third, to about thirty-four thousand. {p} Did Japan's economy collapse? No. After inflation, it grew about nine percent over those twelve years. Slowly, but it grew. What collapsed was the value of the yen in dollars. Same work, same output, fewer dollars.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth (NGDP_RPCH, compounded), population (LP)
shots.title: Slow growth, fewer people
shots.narration: Underneath the yen, there's a slower story too. Since 1995, after inflation, Japan's economy has grown about twenty-five percent. Poland's has more than tripled. {p} And Japan's population peaked in 2011, at about a hundred and twenty-eight million. This year it's about a hundred and twenty-three, and the IMF has a hundred and nineteen by 2031. {pp} The IMF expects Japan to grow well under one percent a year until 2031.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · NGDPDPC (current US$), selected years
shots.title: Already ahead of Japan
shots.narration: Poland isn't the first to close in on Japan in plain dollars. Two of Japan's neighbors already passed it. {p} In 2020, the average South Korean and the average Taiwanese both produced less than the average Japanese person. By 2024, both were ahead. {pp} This year, in the IMF's numbers: South Korea about forty-three and a half thousand dollars per person, Taiwan about forty-four thousand, Japan about thirty-five thousand four hundred. {p} In 1990, Japan was more than three times as rich as Taiwan, in plain dollars, and almost four times as rich as South Korea.

stats.at: South Korea about forty-three and a half thousand
stats.label: South Korea, 2026

stats.at: Japan about thirty-five thousand four hundred
stats.label: Japan, 2026

shots.narration: And if you're enjoying this, the subscribe button is right there. {p} Now, to be fair to Japan: where it still wins.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · unemployment rate (% of labor force), 2026 estimate
shots.title: Unemployment, 2026
shots.narration: Unemployment this year: about two point five percent in Japan, {pp} three point two in Poland. And inflation: in 2022, prices rose two and a half percent in Japan, and more than fourteen percent in Poland. {p} Where Poland wins is debt: about sixty-seven percent of the economy in Poland, about two hundred percent in Japan, one of the highest in the world.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ at market exchange rates (NGDPDPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: So, does Poland pass Japan in plain dollars too? {p} In the IMF's forecast: next year, Japan about thirty-six thousand six hundred dollars per person, Poland about thirty-three thousand three hundred. 2030: forty thousand seven hundred against thirty-nine thousand five hundred. {pp} And 2031: forty-one thousand nine hundred and fifty-three in Japan, forty-one thousand six hundred and ninety-seven in Poland. Two hundred and fifty-six dollars apart. Ninety-nine percent. {p} That's not a pass. It's a coin flip, and it depends on the yen as much as on Poland.

labels.at: forty-one thousand nine hundred and fifty-three
forty-one thousand six hundred and ninety-seven

shots.narration: Think about what that means. In 1990, the average Pole produced six percent of what the average Japanese person did. Today, the average Pole produces about eighty-eight percent of what the average Japanese person does, in the same dollars. {p} And adjusted for what money buys at home, Poland is already ahead. {pp} Japan isn't poor. But in plain money, the gap that defined the last thirty-five years is almost gone.

<soft>So, your guess: does Poland pass Japan in plain dollars by 2031, or does the yen bounce back first?</soft> Tell me in the comments. {p} If you're watching from Japan: does this match what you see in your own wallet? {p} If you're in Poland: did you ever expect to be this close? {p} I read every comment.
And if you missed it, here's the episode where Poland passed Japan, adjusted for prices. It's right here. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

yt.title: Japan Was 16 Times Richer Than Poland. Now It's 14% Ahead.
yt.description:
Income per person in plain US dollars, at market exchange rates (IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026): in 1990 the average Japanese person produced 16× as much as the average Pole ($26,399 vs $1,634). In 2026: $35,400 vs $31,186 — Japan ~14% ahead — and in the IMF's 2031 forecast the gap is $256. Why Japan's dollar income is lower than in 1995 (peak 2012, −32% by 2024 while the real economy grew ~9%: the yen), slow growth and a shrinking population, South Korea and Taiwan already ahead of Japan in plain dollars, and where Japan still wins (unemployment, inflation) and loses (debt ~200% of GDP).
Adjusted for prices (PPP), Poland already passed Japan in 2026 — that's the previous episode.

Sources: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 (NGDPDPC, PPPPC, NGDP_RPCH, LP, LUR, GGXWDG_NGDP, PCPIPCH). 2026+ figures are IMF estimates and forecasts.
